blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Macro & rates, lesson 7: Credit spreads as a risk gauge: investment grade, high yield, and what widening means.

A credit spread is the extra yield a corporate bond pays over a government bond of the same maturity. That gap is the market's price for default risk, and it moves faster than most headlines do. When spreads widen, the market is saying risk is rising, before earnings confirm it, before the rating agencies move.

Split it into two tiers. Investment grade, companies like Royal Bank or Enbridge, typically trades 80 to 150 basis points over the Government of Canada curve in calm conditions. High yield, the riskier tier, sits much wider, often 350 to 500 basis points over, because the chance of default is real and the buyer wants paid for it.

Here is the worked example. In March 2020, the high yield spread in the United States, tracked by the ICE BofA index, blew out from around 360 basis points to over 1,080 basis points in about three weeks. That is not a rounding move, that is the market pricing a wave of defaults. By contrast, investment grade spreads widened too, from roughly 115 to 370, painful, but nowhere near the same multiple. The gap between the two tiers is itself the signal: when high yield widens far more than investment grade, you are watching a flight to quality, not just a rate story. On Thomson ONE, you can pull both indices under fixed income analytics and chart the spread difference directly, rather than staring at two separate yield lines.

The mistake people make is treating spread widening as a timing tool, like it tells you when to sell. It does not. It tells you that risk appetite is deteriorating and that credit markets expect more stress ahead. It says nothing about which week, which stock, or how deep. Plenty of spread-widening episodes reverse within a month. Use it to confirm a thesis about economic stress, not to call a bottom or a top.

Your task today: pull up the current investment grade and high yield spread levels, write down both numbers, and compare them to their five-year average. That tells you whether credit markets are pricing calm or stress right now, which is the evidence base before you ever look at a single stock's technicals.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 31: Estate freeze: mechanics and when it fits.

Here's the problem an estate freeze solves. Your incorporated business owner's company is worth 2 million dollars today. If it grows to 8 million dollars by the time they die, that extra 6 million dollars is all taxed in their hands, at death, in one year, under the deemed disposition rules you already know. That's a massive tax bill landing on one tax return.

An estate freeze locks in today's value for the owner and shifts all future growth to someone else, usually the next generation, without triggering tax now.

Mechanically, here's what happens. The owner exchanges their common shares in the operating company for new fixed-value preferred shares, worth exactly what the common shares were worth, say 2 million dollars. This is done under section 85 or section 86 of the Income Tax Act, using an elected amount so there's no immediate gain. Then new common shares, worth a nominal amount like 100 dollars, are issued to a family trust, or directly to the kids. From that point on, all growth in the business accrues to those new common shares. The owner's preferred shares stay frozen at 2 million dollars. They can retain voting control, keep the right to be paid out, and still draw dividends if the shares are structured that way.

Worked example: owner freezes at 2 million dollars in 2026. By 2040 the company is worth 9 million dollars. The owner's estate still only reports the frozen 2 million dollars of value at death, taxed as a deemed disposition, roughly half included as a capital gain. The other 7 million dollars of growth sits with the kids' common shares, and gets dealt with later, on their own timeline, often using the lifetime capital gains exemption we'll cover next lesson.

The one mistake people make: freezing too early, before the business has any real value, or freezing without a plan for who actually controls the company and the voting shares afterward. A freeze that strips control from the owner while they still need income from the business creates a worse problem than the one it solved.

Communication, lesson 31: Couples: managing two decision makers with different risk appetites.

Olivia Mitchell at the Wharton School studied how couples make retirement decisions and found something advisors ignore at their peril: when spouses disagree on risk, the person who talks more in the meeting tends to win the plan, regardless of whose name is on more of the assets. That's not consensus. That's volume winning over judgment.

Here's the concrete case. A husband wants 80% equities, he's read about long run returns, he's comfortable with drawdowns. His wife wants 40% equities, she remembers 2008, she wants to sleep at night. If you let the husband's confidence set the portfolio at 75% equities, you haven't found a compromise, you've let one person's risk tolerance override the other's. And when the market drops 20%, which it did in early 2020 and again in 2022, she'll remember who talked her into it. Even if returns work out fine, the relationship with your firm doesn't.

The fix: ask each spouse separately, before the joint meeting, two questions. One, what's the maximum percentage drop in your account you could watch happen without wanting to call me. Two, what return are you trying to achieve and by when. Write down both answers with numbers. Then in the joint session, read both answers back verbatim before you propose anything. This does two things. It proves you heard the quieter spouse, and it forces the couple to negotiate their own numbers instead of you averaging them for them.

The one mistake: treating the couple as a single risk profile. Vanguard's own research on couples' advising found mismatched risk tolerance in roughly 70% of couples they studied. If you build one plan for "the household," you've already sided with whoever spoke first.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Nvidia Turmoil Leads a Canadian-Tilted Ten
blocks.script:
Nvidia dominates every feed this morning. The chip giant makes the AI hardware behind most data centres, and CEO Jensen Huang admitted in a memo to employees that he had an affair with a woman identified in reports as a suspected Chinese spy. The board has opened a security probe, shares fell in premarket trading, and Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld told TechCrunch Huang's job odds are roughly a coin flip. The tailwind is Huang's outsized credibility with chip buyers. The headwind is Republican lawmakers demanding he brief Congress this month. An evidence-based advisor says one executive's personal conduct should not move your long-term allocation.

Strathcona Resources is an Alberta oil sands producer majority owned by Waterous Energy Fund. It is buying rival Greenfire Resources in a deal the Globe values at up to two point nine billion dollars, with Greenfire holders choosing cash or stock. The tailwind is scale and reserves. The headwind is Waterous controlling over half of both companies, which thins the float. An advisor says resource consolidation plays belong in a diversified sleeve, not a concentrated bet.

Greenfire Resources is the target, and its shares jumped roughly thirty-six percent in premarket trading per Benzinga on the thirty-nine percent cash premium offered. The tailwind is that premium. The headwind is delisting once the deal closes in early 2027. An advisor says once a takeover premium is priced in, there is little left to chase.

Barrick is one of the world's largest gold miners. Its third quarter profit rose as the Globe reports higher gold prices offset lower output, with central bank buying propping up bullion. The tailwind is gold as an inflation and currency hedge. The headwind is falling production volumes. An advisor says gold miners add volatility without reliably improving a portfolio's long-run return.

AlphaFixe Capital is a Montreal fixed-income manager. It launched what the Globe calls a first-of-its-kind Indigenous reconciliation bond fund, with Sunlife adding it to group retirement plans. The tailwind is a two and a half billion dollar green bond track record to build on. The headwind is proving reconciliation scoring actually changes capital flows. An advisor says values-aligned funds deserve the same fee and performance scrutiny as any other.

Wealthsimple is a Canadian fintech now plugged into Payments Canada's new real-time rail, alongside Questrade. The tailwind is instant settlement after years of delay. The headwind is execution risk in a brand new system. An advisor says faster payments are a convenience upgrade, not a reason to change where you invest.

blocks.title: National Bank's Embark Deal, CIRO Incorporation, Insurer Earnings Dip
blocks.script:
National Bank is buying RESP provider Embark for 226 million dollars, and this is the one to flag for any client with young kids. Wealth Professional reports the deal adds 436,000 RESP beneficiaries and 6 billion dollars in managed assets, making National Bank Canada's sixth-largest bank by this measure. If you've got clients using Embark's group RESP plans, expect servicing changes down the line, and it's worth a proactive call before they hear about it elsewhere.

On the incorporation front, SIMA is backing CIRO's new incorporated approved person model, but it's warning regulators about team ownership. Under the draft rules, as reported by Wealth Professional, the corporation can only have one voting shareholder, the advisor themselves, with no holding companies and no multi-advisor corporations. SIMA wants multiple owners allowed so team practices with smooth succession plans aren't disrupted. If you're an incorporated advisor or thinking about it, this is still moving, watch for the final rule.

Insurers had a rough quarter. Investment Executive reports Canadian insurers saw Q3 net earnings slip, with disability claims weighing on Great-West Lifeco and Manulife in group benefits, while Sun Life's Canadian operations kept growing. For incorporated professionals holding insurance through their corporation, nothing changes in the product mechanics, but it's a reminder to review carrier concentration.

And on the budget, the new Canada Growth Incentive is real money for your business-owner clients. Investment Executive reports it brings a 15 million dollar capital gains exemption on qualifying share sales, available per individual, per business, for shares issued before 2037, plus an expanded small business rollover for reinvested proceeds. If you've got a physician or founder client eyeing a sale or planning succession, this changes the math meaningfully.

blocks.title: Clinics, Grief, and Warnings Across Manitoba Today
blocks.script:
A Steinbach clinic gave rural Manitobans a one-stop shop this week for the kind of paperwork that normally takes a dozen phone calls. CBC Manitoba reports the pop-up service helped people get identification, apply for disability and health benefits, search for housing and employment, and file taxes, all under one roof. For clients in rural practices, this matters: it signals the province is trying to bridge a service gap that usually means a drive to Winnipeg or Brandon. If you have clients or their adult children living outside the Perimeter, this is worth flagging as a resource.

A tougher story out of Brandon. A man has filed a lawsuit against the provincial and federal governments alleging he was sexually abused by a priest at a Brandon residential school nearly six decades ago, and that a Portage la Prairie youth centre worker abused him further. CBC Manitoba has the details. These historic claims continue to surface, and they carry real financial exposure for institutions, something boards with legacy liability concerns should watch.

Closer to home, a 19-year-old pedestrian was killed at a busy intersection on Winnipeg's east side. Her family describes her as full of life, and the death has reignited concern about pedestrian safety at high-traffic crossings, a recurring theme at city hall budget talks.

Police and researchers are warning parents across the Prairies that extremist groups are grooming and radicalizing a growing number of children online, per CBC Manitoba. This is becoming a school-counsellor and parenting conversation, not just a policing one.

blocks.label: Canadian Politics
blocks.title: Budget Grids, Manila Trade, Guns at the Supreme Court
blocks.script:
Start with the budget, because it matters for Manitoba's biggest employer story of the decade. Budget 2026 commits more than fifty billion dollars to expand Canada's electricity system, with the government saying it will connect provincial grids and build thousands of kilometres of transmission lines. But the Globe and Mail reports the budget set aside only tens of millions for studies on interprovincial links, with no new capital for actually building the interties themselves, the lines that would connect Manitoba Hydro to neighbouring grids. That gap between ambition and funding is exactly what grid experts flagged this weekend. Manitoba Hydro is on the watch list here, since any west-to-east or Manitoba-Saskatchewan tie-in depends on federal cost-sharing that hasn't been locked down.

On trade, Mark Carney is on a nine day, four summit tour that pointedly skips Washington. The Globe reports Canada and the Philippines are expected to announce the conclusion of free trade talks when Carney visits Manila this week, part of a broader Indo-Pacific push. He then moves to Cambodia for the Francophonie summit and on to Shenzhen for APEC, where Ottawa says a new strategic partnership with China could unlock seven billion dollars in export markets.

CBC also found Americans living in Canada hopeful the results might help mend economic and cultural ties between the two countries.

blocks.title: New Diabetes Protein Target, Exercise Still Wins
blocks.script: A new study published in Nature Communications identifies a protein called Miro1 as a hidden driver of insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes. Researchers found that Miro1 is elevated in the skeletal muscle of people with type 2 diabetes and may contribute to insulin resistance, potentially making it a target for future treatments. In preclinical models, when researchers removed the protein, insulin responsiveness returned. Here's the part that matters for your training: in a randomized controlled trial involving participants with obesity and type 2 diabetes, they compared the effects of aerobic exercise with those of standard medical care, and exercise lowered Miro1 levels and improved insulin sensitivity. This is still early, the human exercise arm is one trial, but it reinforces something already well established: regular aerobic work does something at the molecular level that medication alone doesn't replicate.

blocks.title: Home bias: Canadian evidence and the right amount of Canada / Deemed disposition at death and the spousal rollover / Talking about death and incapacity: estate conversations that do not feel morbid
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Evidence arsenal, lesson 8: Home bias: Canadian evidence and the right amount of Canada.

Canadian investors hold roughly sixty percent of their equity portfolios in Canadian stocks, according to Vanguard Canada research from 2023. Canada is about three percent of global stock market capitalization. That gap, sixty percent held against three percent available, is home bias, and it is one of the most documented behavioral patterns in finance going back to the French and Poterba studies of the 1990s.

Here is the mechanical problem. The S&P TSX Composite is roughly thirty percent financials and fifteen percent energy. Combined, that is close to half the index in two sectors. The S&P 500 by comparison is about thirty percent technology alone, with financials and energy each under ten percent. So a Canadian-heavy portfolio is not just a geography bet, it is a concentrated sector bet dressed up as a geography bet. Over the ten years ending 2023, the S&P 500 returned about twelve percent annualized in Canadian dollar terms, the TSX about eight percent. Currency did some of that work, but sector composition did more, because global tech carried the decade.

The mistake people make is defending home bias with "I understand these companies" or "the dividends are better." Understanding is not the same as diversification, and TSX dividend yields averaging three percent do not offset a forty-year drag from being underweight the sectors that actually compounded. The evidence does not say zero Canada. It says the sixty percent figure is not a plan, it is a habit, usually built from employer stock, familiarity, and avoiding currency conversion friction.

What this technique reveals: concentration risk hiding inside a home country allocation. What it cannot tell you: the right number for any one household, because that depends on CPP and OAS income already being Canadian-dollar and Canadian-economy exposed, which argues for less home bias, not more, once you count total balance sheet exposure, not just the equity sleeve.

In Thomson ONE, pull the sector weight breakdown for the TSX Composite against the MSCI World index, side by side, and look at the concentration numbers yourself before you argue this with anyone.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 30: Deemed disposition at death and the spousal rollover.

When someone dies in Canada, the Income Tax Act treats them as if they sold everything they own, the moment before death, at fair market value. That's called deemed disposition. It applies to non-registered investments, real estate other than the principal residence, shares in the private corporation, cottage property, everything except what passes to a spouse or common-law partner, or into a qualifying spousal trust. If it passes to the spouse, the deemed disposition happens at the deceased's adjusted cost base instead of fair market value, so no gain is triggered. That's the spousal rollover, under section 70(6) of the Act. Tax doesn't disappear, it defers until the surviving spouse sells or dies.

Here's a worked example. Dr. Patel owns a non-registered investment account, adjusted cost base 200,000 dollars, fair market value 650,000 dollars on the day he dies, in 2026. Unrealized gain is 450,000 dollars. With no spousal rollover, 50 percent of that gain, 225,000 dollars, gets added to his final return as taxable income, taxed at his marginal rate, which at that income level in Manitoba is around 50 percent combined federal and provincial. That's roughly 112,000 dollars of tax on his terminal return, due on the estate.

If instead the account rolls to his wife, Manitoba allows that transfer at the 200,000 dollar cost base. No gain is realized now. She inherits his cost base and the tax bill moves down the road to her eventual sale or death.

The one mistake people make: assuming the rollover is automatic and unconditional for any asset left to a spouse. It only applies if the property actually vests indefeasibly in the spouse, or in a spousal trust meeting strict conditions, within 36 months of death. A poorly drafted will, a discretionary trust that gives the spouse less than full entitlement, or assets left partly to kids, can disqualify the rollover on that portion.

Communication, lesson 30: Talking about death and incapacity: estate conversations that do not feel morbid.

Susan Bradley, who built the field of financial transitions planning, noticed something in her clients at Sudden Money Institute. The ones who had already talked through death and incapacity before a crisis hit recovered their footing in weeks. The ones who hadn't took years. The difference wasn't the money. It was whether the conversation had already happened.

Here's the mistake almost every advisor makes: they frame the conversation as being about death. It isn't. It's about control. The moment you say "let's talk about what happens if you die," the client's brain flags danger and shuts half the room down. Reframe it as "let's talk about who makes decisions if you can't," and the same content lands as competence, not doom.

Worked example. A client, 68, has a $2.1 million portfolio and a healthcare proxy he signed in 2009, seventeen years ago, naming a brother who died in 2019. You don't say "your estate plan has a problem." You say, "If you were in a hospital bed next Tuesday, who picks up the phone and tells the doctor what you'd want?" He stops. He doesn't have an answer. That silence is the work. You're not discussing mortality tables, you're surfacing a gap he can fix in one phone call to his attorney. Now the conversation has a next action instead of a feeling.

The mistake to avoid: leading with statistics. Advisors love to open with "70% of Americans don't have an updated will" (a figure Caring.com has reported in various years, including 2024). Stats make the client feel like a category, not a person, and they shut down faster than if you'd said nothing. Lead with the decision, not the data.

Communication: Pick one current client. Write the single sentence you'd use to open this topic with them, framed around control and decisions, not death. Read it aloud once before your next meeting.

blocks.title: Gildan Plunges, Musk Loses Billions, BCE Spends Big
blocks.script:
Gildan Activewear leads the board today. The Montreal clothing maker makes t-shirts and basics for retailers across North America. The Globe reports shares plunged twenty five percent after the company missed third quarter estimates and cut its full year revenue forecast to a range of five point four to five point five billion dollars. Higher borrowing costs and inflation hit harder than analysts expected. The tailwind is a cheap valuation after the drop. The headwind is a guidance cut investors rarely forgive quickly. An evidence based advisor tells a client this is a single stock story, not a reason to abandon a diversified equity sleeve.

Elon Musk runs Tesla and SpaceX, the electric car and rocket companies tied to his Texas business empire. He is in the news after spending nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates in this week's midterms, bets that mostly failed as Democrats took both chambers of Congress. The tailwind is his enormous personal wealth cushioning any loss. The headwind is a resurgent Democratic Congress now eyeing investigations into his companies. An advisor says political spending by a founder is noise, what matters is Tesla and SpaceX fundamentals, not who he backs.

BCE, the parent of Bell Canada, is next. The telecom giant posted third quarter results showing free cash flow falling as capital spending jumped nearly fifty percent on artificial intelligence data centres and United States fibre networks, per the Globe. Mobile subscriber growth stalled. The tailwind is a long term bet on data infrastructure demand. The headwind is a weaker dividend cushion if free cash flow keeps sliding. An advisor tells income focused clients to watch payout sustainability closely before adding to a position.

Airbnb rounds out the top names. The short term rental platform raised its revenue growth forecast, citing strong global demand and a rebound in corporate travel, the Globe reports. blocks.title: Budget's Growth Incentive, RRSP Overhaul, CIRO Bars Advisor
blocks.script:
Budget 2026 landed yesterday, and the piece that actually changes your client conversations is buried in the tax measures. Ottawa's new Canada Growth Incentive lets founders, employees and outside investors shelter up to fifteen million dollars in capital gains on qualifying shares of Canadian controlled private corporations with a hundred million dollars or less in assets, held at least three years. For an incorporated business owner planning an exit, that moves after tax proceeds on a fifteen million dollar gain from about seventy one percent to ninety six percent. There's also an expanded small business rollover for reinvested proceeds, so revisit any sale timeline sitting on a client's desk this month.

On retirement, the budget proposes what's being called an RRSP for life: the account could stay open past seventy one instead of forcing a RRIF conversion, though minimum withdrawals would still start at that age. That follows CALU and the Canadian Forum for Financial Markets pushing Ottawa to raise the RRSP contribution age to seventy five. Also note the personal tax filing deadline is moving to May fifteenth. Update client calendars now, not in April.

On the regulatory side, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, CIRO, has permanently barred a British Columbia advisor who impersonated a client to mortgage that client's own home, forging transfers and loans. He's fined five hundred thousand dollars and ordered to pay over four hundred forty two thousand in disgorgement. CIRO has also scheduled a new sanctions hearing for advisor Michael Jordan MacDonnell. Useful if a client ever asks whether the regulator has teeth.

Wealthsimple launched an AI assistant called Penny that can move money, place trades and rebalance portfolios, with every transaction still needing client sign off, and the firm plans to open the tool to third party AI access by 2027. Expect independent minded clients to ask you about it.

For anyone in a life transition, a Wealth Professional report found fewer than one in three caregivers had any financial discussion or plan before the responsibility landed on them. If a client mentions an aging parent, that's your cue to start the eldercare conversation now, not during the crisis.

And on the watch list: the Bank of Canada's first rate hike in more than three years landed a week before this budget, so expect fixed income and mortgage renewal questions at your next client meeting.

blocks.script:
Prime Minister Mark Carney tabled his second budget yesterday, and the scale is the story. The 2026 federal budget, released Thursday, says the government plans to reform the Temporary Foreign Worker Program. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne framed it around affordability and what he called economic sovereignty. On the spending side, CBC reports the budget pledges $50 billion over a decade on programs and services for Indigenous peoples in key sectors like on-reserve infrastructure, housing, education, health care, child welfare, policing and emergency management, plus more than $50 billion in bold and ambitious measures to expand Canada's electricity system. On immigration, the plan looks to maintain broad targets for permanent and temporary resident admissions while offering permanent status to up to 200,000 longtime temporary residents who have already applied, on top of the existing 380,000 annual permanent resident target.

Critics are focused on the debt side. CBC's analysis frames this as Carney betting he can borrow now and invest for growth, with risk if those bets don't pay off, leaving Canada's debt load exposed. Opposition voices argue that record spending shifts the burden onto younger Canadians who'll service the debt later, a framing you'll hear repeated in coming weeks as the fiscal tables get parsed.

Away from Ottawa, on the watch list: Elections Alberta told a legislature committee the Oct. 19 referendum cost just over $84 million to execute, with chief electoral officer Gordon McClure requesting an additional $49 million on top of the $34 million already spent from the $51-million budget for 2026-27. It's a live number for anyone watching the separatist file bleed into provincial finances.

blocks.script:
Start with the Winnipeg Jets, because what happened this week borders on disbelief. Tuesday night in Montreal, the Jets trailed the Canadiens by four goals with under three minutes left in regulation, then scored three times to force overtime and won it. blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Real estate and REITs: cap rates, FFO, and interest rate sensitivity / Trusts: testamentary, alter ego, and family trusts, and the 21 year rule / Explaining fees: the conversation most advisors avoid
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Industry structure, lesson 8: Real estate and REITs: cap rates, FFO, and interest rate sensitivity.

A real estate investment trust does not earn income the way a normal company does, and net income actively misleads you here. The reason is depreciation. Buildings get depreciated on the income statement every year, but good buildings often appreciate in real terms. So the industry built its own metric: funds from operations, FFO. Take net income, add back real estate depreciation and amortization, subtract gains on property sales. That's the cash the trust is actually generating from operating real estate.

Take a concrete case. Say a REIT reports net income of 200 million dollars, with 150 million in depreciation and amortization and a 20 million gain from selling a property. FFO equals 200 plus 150 minus 20, which is 330 million dollars. If there are 100 million shares outstanding, FFO per share is 3.30 dollars. Compare that to a reported earnings per share of maybe 2.00 dollars and you see how distorted the raw number was. In Thomson ONE, FFO and FFO per share usually sit in the REIT-specific template under the financials tab, not buried in the standard earnings line.

Now the cap rate. That's net operating income divided by property value. A cap rate of 5 percent on a building generating 10 million in net operating income implies a value of 200 million. Cap rates move inversely with long-term rates. When the 10-year Treasury yield rises, cap rates tend to follow with a lag, and implied property values fall, even if rents haven't moved yet. That's the interest rate sensitivity: REITs carry real debt, refinance on a schedule, and compete for capital against bonds yielding more.

The common mistake is using price to earnings on a REIT and concluding it looks expensive or cheap. P/E on a REIT is close to meaningless because depreciation inflates the denominator's distortion. Always reprice against FFO or price to FFO instead.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 29: Trusts: testamentary, alter ego, and family trusts, and the 21 year rule.

Every trust you set up for a client has a clock running on it, and most people never think about it until it's a problem. That clock is the 21 year rule, and it exists so people can't dodge tax forever by holding assets in a trust instead of an individual's hands.

Here's the mechanism. On every 21st anniversary of a trust's creation, the trust is deemed to have disposed of all its capital property at fair market value, and reacquired it at that same value. Any accrued gain gets taxed inside the trust, at the top marginal rate, unless the trustees distribute the assets out to beneficiaries before that date.

Three trust types you'll see constantly. A testamentary trust is created by a will, comes into existence on death, and since 2016 no longer gets graduated tax rates, except for a graduated rate estate in its first 36 months. An alter ego trust is for people 65 and older: they transfer assets in on a tax deferred rollover basis, they're the sole beneficiary while alive, and the 21 year clock starts the day it's created, not the day they die. A family trust, often used by incorporated business owners for income splitting or an estate freeze, also has the clock running from inception.

Worked example. A business owner in Winnipeg sets up a family trust in 2005 holding shares of a holding company worth 500,000 dollars at the time, now worth 3 million. The 21st anniversary lands in 2026, this year. If the trustees do nothing, the trust is deemed to sell those shares for 3 million, triggering a 2.5 million dollar capital gain taxed at the trust's top rate, roughly 50 percent in Manitoba on the taxable half. That's over 600,000 dollars in tax, inside the trust, with no beneficiary rollover available.

The one mistake: nobody diarizes the anniversary date. Trustees forget trusts aren't permanent, and a trust set up in 2005 has its deadline hit in 2026, this exact year, with no warning letter from anyone.

Communication, lesson 29: Explaining fees: the conversation most advisors avoid.

A behavioral finance researcher named Meir Statman studied why clients rate fee conversations as the moment they trust an advisor least, even when the fee is fair. His finding: it is not the number that creates suspicion, it is the framing. When advisors explain fees in isolation, as in "I charge one percent," the client's brain has nothing to compare it to except zero. Zero always wins. So the client hears a cost with no attached benefit.

Here is the fix, with real numbers. Say a client has 800,000 dollars invested, and your fee is one percent, so 8,000 dollars a year. Instead of stating that number alone, you say: "On 800,000 dollars, you're paying about 8,000 dollars this year. For that, I'm managing the allocation across fourteen holdings, rebalancing twice a year, and I ran the Monte Carlo projection last month that showed your plan holds up in 90 percent of market scenarios through 2045. If you did this yourself and got the allocation wrong by even a few percentage points over a decade, Vanguard's own research on advisor value, the Advisor's Alpha study, puts that behavioral cost at roughly 1.5 to 3 percent a year in lost returns." You're not justifying a cost. You're pricing a service against a specific alternative.

The one mistake: advisors apologize before they explain. They say "I know fees are frustrating, but..." That sentence primes the client to feel resentment before you've said a single number. Statman's research and later work by Daniel Crosby both show that the apology frame, not the fee frame, is what triggers the client to start shopping for a cheaper advisor.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pick one REIT in Thomson ONE, pull net income, depreciation, and any property sale gains from the last annual filing, and calculate FFO per share by hand. Compare it to reported EPS and note the gap.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull the trust deeds or will copies for any client files where you know a trust exists, find the settlement date, calculate the 21st anniversary, and flag any landing within the next 24 months for a planning conversation.

Communication: Write out your own fee explanation using an actual client's account size, following the exact structure above: the dollar figure, the specific service list, and one external comparison point. Say it out loud once before your next client meeting.

lessons.title: Trusts: testamentary, alter ego, and family trusts, and the 21 year rule
lessons.script:
Every trust you set up for a client has a clock running on it, and most people never think about it until it's a problem. That clock is the 21 year rule, and it exists so people can't dodge tax forever by holding assets in a trust instead of an individual's hands.

Here's the mechanism. On every 21st anniversary of a trust's creation, the trust is deemed to have disposed of all its capital property at fair market value, and reacquired it at that same value. Any accrued gain gets taxed inside the trust, at the top marginal rate, unless the trustees distribute the assets out to beneficiaries before that date.

Three trust types you'll see constantly. A testamentary trust is created by a will, comes into existence on death, and since 2016 no longer gets graduated tax rates, except for a graduated rate estate in its first 36 months. An alter ego trust is for people 65 and older: they transfer assets in on a tax deferred rollover basis, they're the sole beneficiary while alive, and the 21 year clock starts the day it's created, not the day they die. A family trust, often used by incorporated business owners for income splitting or an estate freeze, also has the clock running from inception.

Worked example. A business owner in Winnipeg sets up a family trust in 2005 holding shares of a holding company worth 500,000 dollars at the time, now worth 3 million. The 21st anniversary lands in 2026, this year. If the trustees do nothing, the trust is deemed to sell those shares for 3 million, triggering a 2.5 million dollar capital gain taxed at the trust's top rate, roughly 50 percent in Manitoba on the taxable half. That's over 600,000 dollars in tax, inside the trust, with no beneficiary rollover available.

The one mistake: nobody diarizes the anniversary date. Trustees forget trusts aren't permanent, and a trust set up in 2005 has its deadline hit in 2026, this exact year, with no warning letter from anyone.
lessons.task: Pull the trust deeds or will copies for any client files where you know a trust exists, find the settlement date, calculate the 21st anniversary, and flag any landing within the next 24 months for a planning conversation.

lessons.label: Communication
lessons.title: Explaining fees: the conversation most advisors avoid
lessons.script:
A behavioral finance researcher named Meir Statman studied why clients rate fee conversations as the moment they trust an advisor least, even when the fee is fair. His finding: it is not the number that creates suspicion, it is the framing. When advisors explain fees in isolation, as in "I charge one percent," the client's brain has nothing to compare it to except zero. Zero always wins. So the client hears a cost with no attached benefit.

Here is the fix, with real numbers. Say a client has 800,000 dollars invested, and your fee is one percent, so 8,000 dollars a year. Instead of stating that number alone, you say: "On 800,000 dollars, you're paying about 8,000 dollars this year. For that, I'm managing the allocation across fourteen holdings, rebalancing twice a year, and I ran the Monte Carlo projection last month that showed your plan holds up in 90 percent of market scenarios through 2045. If you did this yourself and got the allocation wrong by even a few percentage points over a decade, Vanguard's own research on advisor value, the Advisor's Alpha study, puts that behavioral cost at roughly 1.5 to 3 percent a year in lost returns." You're not justifying a cost. You're pricing a service against a specific alternative.

The one mistake: advisors apologize before they explain. They say "I know fees are frustrating, but..." That sentence primes the client to feel resentment before you've said a single number. Statman's research and later work by Daniel Crosby both show that the apology frame, not the fee frame, is what triggers the client to start shopping for a cheaper advisor.
lessons.task: Write out your own fee explanation using an actual client's account size, following the exact structure above: the dollar figure, the specific service list, and one external comparison point. Say it out loud once before your next client meeting.
lessons.drill: Record yourself explaining your fee in under ninety seconds, using a real or sample account size. Score it on three items: did you state the dollar figure before any qualifier or apology, did you name at least two concrete services tied to that fee, and did you include one outside comparison point with a named source. Three out of three is a pass. Two or fewer, rerecord.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Earnings, Rate Hikes and a Post-Midterm World
blocks.script:
Good evening. Here's The Ten for November 5th, 2026.

The Bank of England raised interest rates today for the first time since 2023, and signalled more hikes could follow. The central bank warned inflation is likely to climb to around 5 per cent by the middle of next year, putting policymakers in the uncomfortable position of tightening even as price pressures build.

Closer to home, Canada's trade surplus widened to its highest level in more than four years in September, hitting 5.35 billion dollars. Gold and energy exports, mostly headed to the United States, did the heavy lifting.

On the political front, our Business Brief looks at how the Democratic wave in Tuesday's U.S. midterms is rippling into Canadian boardrooms, with corporate profits sitting at levels not seen since 1929, a striking backdrop for a changing Washington.

In energy, Shell has pledged more than 210 million dollars to oil exploration off the coast of Newfoundland after winning six exploration licences. The provincial regulator says it received ten successful bids in total, the largest number since 2000.

In tech, the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board has put 50 million dollars into Toronto-based Beacon Software, a fast-growing AI company. It's a rare direct bet from CPPIB's growth equity arm, which has previously backed Cohere and Wealthsimple.

Earnings season rolled on. TC Energy beat profit estimates on strength in its U.S. gas pipeline business. Canadian Natural Resources topped expectations on higher oil prices and output. Nutrien, WSP Global, South Bow, MDA Space and Bombardier also reported. MDA Space posted nearly 31 million dollars in quarterly profit and raised its guidance. WSP Global's profit climbed to 333.7 million dollars on higher revenue. South Bow earned 99 million dollars, edging up from a year ago.

Bombardier raised its cash forecast and delivered 33 jets in the quarter, with revenue up 3 per cent to 2.37 billion U.S. dollars. Still, questions are mounting over how the company plans to deploy its growing cash pile.

Our commentary desk looks at what comes next after this week's midterms, dubbing it the post-Trump era, even though Trump himself still has 26 more months in office. Related commentary argues younger Canadians will ultimately foot the bill for Ottawa's spending and borrowing as the population ages.

Finally, the midterm results are raising hopes of tariff relief for Canada's aluminum sector, after 50 per cent tariffs pushed some producers to redirect shipments to Europe. Broader trade talks between Ottawa and Washington may also get new momentum.
talkingPoints: One, central banks are diverging, with the Bank of England hiking into rising inflation while other economies ease.
Two, Canada's trade numbers are being propped up by gold and energy, not broad-based strength.
Three, earnings season shows resource and infrastructure names outperforming, led by TC Energy and Canadian Natural.
Four, Bombardier's cash position is strong, but investors want clarity on capital deployment.
Five, the political shift in Washington could open a window for tariff relief on Canadian aluminum and broader trade talks.

blocks.title: PWL's New President, OAS Snags, Year-End Tax Moves
blocks.script:
Start with PWL Capital. The firm has named Ben Felix as president, while he keeps his chief investment officer title and his Rational Reminder podcast work. PWL Capital hands its chief investment officer the president title, with two leaders now splitting every decision at a firm managing more than 8 billion dollars for Canadian households. For a Winnipeg advisor, this is a signal that evidence-based, fee-only shops are formalizing succession and governance, something clients at bank wealth arms will ask you to compare against.

On OAS, Globe Advisor flags a real operational problem. Service Canada is enrolling some seniors for Old Age Security automatically at the age of 65 even though they requested a deferral, creating headaches for those who still earn income and want to maximize the pension's benefits. Advisors report Service Canada is taking up to a year or more to process their clients' deferral requests, meaning clients end up calling to reverse enrolment and figuring out what to do with payments already received. If you have clients still working past 65, check their MSCA account now, don't assume a deferral request was actioned.

Year-end tax planning for incorporated business owners. The Globe lays out mechanics worth repeating today. Buy and put assets into use before December 14, since "available for use" means a laptop still in its box at year-end won't count this year. Consider hiring family: pay a lower-income spouse or kids a reasonable salary for working in the business, the business deducts it, they pay less tax than you, and they build RRSP room and CPP eligibility. For incorporated professionals, remember the small business deduction means the tax rate on active business income averages just 10.8 per cent across Canada in 2026 and 10.6 per cent in 2027, much lower than personal tax rates anywhere in the country, so timing of bonuses versus dividends still matters, and watch for alternative minimum tax exposure before you pull the trigger.
talkingPoints: PWL Capital's Ben Felix is now president as well as CIO, a governance signal from the fee-only side.
If your client deferred OAS past 65, confirm with Service Canada directly, auto-enrolment errors are being reported.
Put new equipment into use before December 14 for it to count this tax year.
Hiring your spouse or kids in the business can shift income and build their RRSP room.
A third of Canadians couldn't cover a 2,000 dollar shock, a reminder to stress-test every plan.

blocks.title: Tariffs, Hangar Jobs, and Council Shake-up
blocks.script:
Premier Wab Kinew is calling on American lawmakers to drop tariffs on Canada now that Democrats have taken control of both chambers of Congress. Kinew congratulated Democrats for what he called dominating Trump in Tuesday's midterms, and his office is framing the result as an opening to push Washington on trade. For anyone with clients in export-exposed sectors, that's a storyline worth watching through the budget cycle.

Closer to home, Mayor Scott Gillingham has named his five member executive policy committee. Two rookie councillors have joined Winnipeg Mayor Scott Gillingham's inner circle, while two returning members take on new roles and finance committee chair Jeff Browaty keeps his job. That's the group setting the city's agenda, including property tax and development decisions, for the next four years.

On the jobs front, a 73,110 square foot maintenance hangar being built near Winnipeg's airport will create hundreds of jobs and the potential for more flights, according to WestJet's CEO. That's a meaningful capital investment landing right in Winnipeg's backyard.

Less positive: the Manitoba government has shut down a trucking company for a second time, the same operator tied to the deadly May crash in Brandon that prompted calls for a crackdown on companies who move jurisdictions or change names to dodge safety regulations.

blocks.title: Charity Rules Overhaul and Hydro's Drought Loss
blocks.script: The Canada Revenue Agency and Finance Canada have opened a consultation on overhauling the rules for registered charities. Canadian registered charities have until December 3, 2026, to weigh in on proposed changes that could reshape how charities interact with the CRA. The review touches disbursement quotas and whether the rules should be tightened where a revoked charity transfers assets to a closely related or newly established charity, thereby reducing the amount subject to the revocation tax. It also asks whether the CRA should make more information about charity audits and compliance outcomes publicly available, particularly where serious non-compliance results in a penalty, suspension or revocation. That's the biggest governance shake-up for Canadian charities in years, worth flagging to any client who sits on a board.
talkingPoints: CRA's charity rules consultation closes December 3rd, flag it to board-sitting clients.

blocks.label: AI & Technology
blocks.title: AMD's Canadian Bet, Google's AI School Backlash
blocks.script:
AMD is paying about two point nine billion US dollars for Taalas, the Toronto chip startup that builds silicon custom-wired to specific AI models. The Globe and Mail reports this ranks among the largest takeovers of a Canadian tech company ever, behind only the Ecolab purchase of CoolIT Systems in March. The Taalas team stays in Toronto, joining AMD's existing Canadian workforce. For your clients in tech or venture, this is the pattern to watch: build smart in Canada, sell to the Americans. It's good for founders and employees, less good if you want Canada to own the next Nvidia.

Google is in a public fight over AI in schools. It's letting school boards switch off its AI tools, but only if they also give up Google Search entirely. Politicians including New York's mayor and a former Federal Trade Commission chair are calling that coercive, bundling a monopoly product with AI adoption.

blocks.title: Menopause Costs, Dating Violence Alert, and Muscle Repair
blocks.script:
A House of Commons committee heard this week that unmanaged menopause symptoms cost Canada's economy an estimated 3.5 billion dollars a year. The Menopause Foundation and Deloitte Canada estimate about 540,000 work days are lost each year in Canada owing to managing symptoms, with women over 40 now a quarter of the labour force. For clients in that age bracket, this is a retirement planning conversation, not just a health one: reduced hours or early exits from the workforce show up directly in savings trajectories.

Separately, new pediatric guidance says a third of Canadian youth have faced dating violence, from physical and sexual abuse to online harassment. Doctors are being told to screen for it starting now.
talkingPoints: Menopause symptom costs are now a documented workforce and retirement planning issue, not just a health footnote.
One in three young Canadians report dating violence, a stat worth knowing if you have teen or young adult clients.
A new muscle repair compound showed promise in mice, early days, not a human therapy yet.
Regulatory licensing delays in a high profile pediatric case are raising oversight questions in Ontario.
Worth flagging to clients: employer benefits plans increasingly need menopause and mental health coverage review.

blocks.label: Parenting
blocks.title: Manitoba Childcare Gap, CCB Rises Slightly
blocks.script: A Winnipeg news conference this week put a number on something families already feel. The Child Care Coalition of Manitoba says the province needs 77,000 more licensed spaces to hit the national access benchmark of 59 percent coverage. Susan Prentice of the coalition says Manitoba needs to add 23,000 infant and preschool spaces and 54,000 school-age spaces to hit that target. The coalition credits the province for progress on 10 dollar a day care, new spaces, and higher wages for early childhood educators. But the gap is real, and for clients juggling parental leave timing against a return to work, waitlists are still the binding constraint, not benefit cheques. On the benefit side, the Canada Child Benefit rose two percent this past July, a smaller bump than 2025's 2.7 percent, reflecting cooling inflation.
talkingPoints: Manitoba childcare shortfall now measured at 77,000 spaces, a Winnipeg coalition says.
Waitlists remain the real barrier to parents returning to work, not benefit amounts.

Royal Bank has raised its dividend every year it's been allowed to for over a decade, and that single fact is the entire case for why the dividend discount model still earns its place on a Canadian large cap desk, even after everything you've learned about discount rates and terminal value.

Here's the logic. For a mature, regulated, cash generative business, the dividend isn't a residual. It's management's own forecast of sustainable earnings power, vetted by a board that knows the market punishes a cut harder than almost any other signal. So instead of forecasting free cash flow and fighting with terminal value assumptions, you let the company tell you what it believes it can pay forever.

Work the numbers with Royal Bank. Pull the trailing twelve month dividend from Thomson ONE, it's sitting around 5.72 Canadian dollars annualized as of late 2026. Royal's five year dividend growth rate, also on Thomson ONE under the dividend history tab, runs close to 7 percent. Your cost of equity, built the way you built it in lesson one of this cycle using a risk free rate off the ten year Government of Canada bond plus an equity risk premium, lands around 9 percent for a Canadian bank.

Gordon growth model: value equals next year's dividend divided by cost of equity minus growth. Next year's dividend is 5.72 times 1.07, so 6.12. Divide by 0.09 minus 0.07, that's 0.02. You get 306 dollars a share. Royal trades nowhere near that, which tells you immediately the growth assumption is too generous for a model this sensitive, not that the stock is wildly mispriced.

That's the one mistake. The denominator is cost of equity minus growth, and when those two numbers sit close together, small changes in either one swing the output by tens of dollars. People quote a DDM value with false precision and forget it's a knife edge calculation, not a point estimate.

The model's honest use is as a sanity check on dividend sustainability and a cross reference against your DCF, not a standalone price target.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 28: Beneficiary designations: registered plans, insurance, and common mistakes.

Here's the story nobody tells clients until it's too late. A woman in Winnipeg dies in 2024 with a seven hundred thousand dollar RRSP. Her will, updated after her divorce, leaves everything to her two adult kids. But her RRSP beneficiary form still names her ex husband from 2009. Guess who gets the money. The ex husband. The will is irrelevant here, because a beneficiary designation on a registered plan or an insurance policy overrides the will completely. This is the single most common and most expensive mistake I see.

Here's why it matters beyond the shock value. In Manitoba, assets with a valid, properly named beneficiary, like RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs, and life insurance, bypass your estate and avoid probate entirely. We covered probate fees last lesson, roughly seven hundred dollars per hundred thousand of estate value in Manitoba. So naming a beneficiary directly isn't just about who gets the money, it's a probate saving tool too. But that same feature becomes a trap when the form is stale.

Worked example. Client has a TFSA worth 95,000 dollars in 2026. If no beneficiary is named, it falls into the estate, gets probated, and is divided per the will, taking months. If a spouse is named as successor holder, the TFSA transfers directly to them, tax free, same day essentially, no probate, no estate involvement. One line on a form changes the entire outcome.

The one mistake: people update their will after a divorce, remarriage, or death in the family, and assume that covers everything. It does not. Beneficiary forms live separately with the financial institution and the insurance company, and nobody automatically syncs them with your will.

Communication, lesson 28: Handling the expert client: the physician who has read the study.

A cardiologist client once told his advisor, bluntly, that he'd read the Morningstar paper on sequence of returns risk and didn't think the advisor's withdrawal strategy accounted for it. The advisor's instinct was to defend the plan. Bad move. The right move, the one that actually worked, was to say: "Walk me through what you took from it." That single sentence changed the entire dynamic of the meeting.

Here's the concept. Expert clients, physicians especially, are trained to pattern-match on data and to distrust authority that isn't backed by evidence. Atul Gawande has written about this directly: doctors are taught checklist thinking, and they apply that same scrutiny to every professional they hire. When you respond to their research with reassurance instead of engagement, you read as evasive, even if you're right. The guide's job isn't to win the argument. It's to locate exactly where their understanding and yours diverge, then close that specific gap.

The mistake is treating the client's knowledge as a threat to manage rather than a resource to use. Advisors often respond to a client citing a study with a generic rebuttal, "past performance doesn't guarantee future results," which is true and also insulting to someone who already knows that. It signals you didn't actually listen to what they read.

In the real case, the advisor asked the cardiologist to name the specific finding. Turned out the client had the right concept but the wrong application: he thought sequence risk meant avoiding equities entirely in year one of retirement, when the actual research, from Wade Pfau among others, points toward a bond tent or dynamic withdrawal rate instead. The advisor could now teach from inside the client's own framework, not against it.

blocks.title: Shopify Slips, Foodtastic Pounces, Maple Leaf Squeezed
blocks.script:
Shopify leads today. The Ottawa based e-commerce platform that powers millions of online storefronts posted third quarter revenue of three point seven four billion dollars, missing analyst estimates even as profit rose, and the stock fell on the Toronto exchange. The Globe reports customers are starting to use AI agents to make purchases through the platform. Tailwind: higher profit and AI integration deals. Headwind: a growth story investors now expect to beat, not just meet. An evidence based advisor would tell a client not to trade a single quarter's miss, valuation already prices in a lot of future growth.

MTY Food Group and its suitor Foodtastic are next. MTY owns Thai Express, Wetzel's Pretzels and Manchu Wok, and Foodtastic has tabled a hostile, roughly nine hundred eighty two million dollar takeover bid. The Globe reports MTY replaced chief executive Eric Lefebvre with board member Victor Mandel the same week the bid landed. Tailwind: a premium offer forces the board to prove MTY's standalone value. Headwind: leadership churn mid takeover looks messy to shareholders. An advisor would say: don't chase the headline price, wait to see if a higher bid or a real defence materializes.

Maple Leaf Foods is in the news on weaker numbers. The Mississauga based protein and packaged foods company saw third quarter profit from continuing operations fall to twenty two point three million dollars from twenty three point three million a year earlier, even as sales edged higher, per the Globe. Tailwind: top line growth continues. Headwind: margins are being squeezed. An advisor would say this is a steady, low volatility holding, not a growth story, size it accordingly.

Suncor Energy beat expectations. The Calgary oil sands major posted adjusted operating profit of three dollars and ninety seven cents a share for the quarter ended September thirtieth, topping estimates, the Globe reports. Tailwind: strong execution and production. Headwind: it's still a commodity price taker. An advisor would say energy names like this belong in a diversified sleeve, not as a standalone bet on oil prices.
talkingPoints: Shopify's miss is a valuation story, not a business breakdown.
Foodtastic versus MTY is turning into a real board fight, watch for a bump.
Maple Leaf's margins, not its sales line, are the thing to track.
Suncor's beat shows execution still matters more than oil price swings.
The Cloth case is a reminder to check who actually holds your money.

blocks.title: OAS Shrinks, Mirabaud Deal, CCPC Rate Watch
blocks.script:
The Globe reports Old Age Security now covers a shrinking slice of retirees' income, and pairs that with fresh advice on CPP timing. The specific question the Globe raises: should someone turning 65 start Canada Pension Plan benefits in December or wait until 2027. Their reporting notes that by delaying payments, a soon-to-be 65-year-old will be temporarily "underwater," but the catch-up period is not very long. If you have clients hitting 65 this quarter, have that conversation now, before year-end deadlines close in.

On the deal front, Nour Private Wealth has completed its acquisition of Mirabaud Canada's wealth management business, closing October 30. The announcement frames it around family office services, tax efficiency, estate planning, and succession for ultra-high-net-worth clients. For independents here in Winnipeg, it is another marker of consolidation at the top end of private wealth, worth noting if you refer high-net-worth files out of province.

On regulation, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization has scheduled a settlement hearing for advisor Mazhar Hussain Malik. No outcome yet, but flag it if you have any client overlap with his book.

You already heard the federal budget drops this week with small-business measures as a centerpiece. Your angle: the Canadian Federation of Independent Business is pushing hard, right up to budget day, to cut the federal small-business rate from 9 percent, stuck there since 2019, down to 6 percent. For incorporated physicians and other professional corporations, that rate drives passive income and retained earnings planning directly. Watch Thursday for whether Ottawa touches that rate or the $500,000 small-business limit.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: New Council, Sewage Probe, Flood Aid, Child Care Gap
blocks.script:
A new Winnipeg city council was sworn in this week after the most turnover in recent memory, and the agenda is already taking shape. Global News reports Mayor Scott Gillingham and all fifteen councillors took the Declaration of Office Tuesday. The Free Press editorial board is already watching what it calls the "Gang of Nine" and whether this council does business as usual. For boards and committees, expect new faces pushing harder on homelessness, with one national activist telling the Free Press the political conditions here could actually produce progress this term.

On the sewage spill, the city has new details. Tim Shanks, the water and waste director, told CBC the bypass gates that dumped nearly ten million litres of partially treated sewage into the Red River Monday were never supposed to open on their own. The wrong default settings at the new treatment plant helped cause the spill, with gates that are supposed to be in manual mode left in automatic. The city estimates the spill lasted about two hours and 37 minutes. Physical lockouts are now installed on the gates so they can't open automatically again. This comes as the city works through a multi-billion dollar treatment plant upgrade, so expect questions about oversight.

On flooding, CBC reports families northwest of Winnipeg are still waiting to hear what provincial funding they'll get, months after a June storm filled basements. Funding for basic and essential needs under the flood recovery program is capped at three million dollars per claim, minus the deductible, up to the assessed value of the property. The gap between need and insurance coverage is still a live issue for rural clients.

On child care, the Manitoba Child Care Coalition says the province needs seventy-seven thousand more spaces to hit the national access benchmark, a number worth having ready for any workforce or HR conversation.

blocks.title: Youth Climate Trial, Charity Compliance Warnings
blocks.script:
The biggest story for you today comes out of a Vancouver courtroom, where Canada's first youth-led climate trial moved into its second week. UBC climate scientist Simon Donner testified that Canada does not need to shut down its industries or take a catastrophic financial hit to effectively fight climate change. He told the court there's also benefits, because that means the new technologies are things that can also make you money. Fifteen plaintiffs aged 17 to 25 argue Ottawa's climate response violates their constitutional rights, government witnesses take the stand this week, and closing arguments wait until February.

Two things heard elsewhere connect to that case. Witnesses already told MPs the federal fast-track bill threatens environmental review, and Hydro-Québec's own supply plan admits it may need to import power from the US and other provinces within three years.

On governance, Global News reports the CRA pulled Food Banks of Saskatchewan's charitable status over a missed annual filing. It lands right after the CRA stopped pre-approving changes to charitable purposes, pushing more compliance risk onto boards.

blocks.title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
blocks.script:
Start with the number that should worry every client holding crypto. Binance says the engineers behind a six point three billion dollar hack were lured through fake job interviews, contacted on a legitimate job platform and walked through bogus interviews with fake company reps, per the BBC. That is social engineering at the executive level, not a code exploit. If you have clients in digital assets, this is the line to use: the weak point is people, not blockchains.

On identity and fraud, Anthropic is building a system called FlashProve, letting anyone verify an AI response actually came from the model it claims to be from, TechCrunch reports. That matters as voice and text deepfakes get better, and it is worth mentioning to clients worried about impersonation scams targeting their accounts.
talkingPoints: Binance heist shows fraud risk is now about fake job offers, not stolen passwords.

blocks.title: Menopause Care Gaps and a Heart-Healthy Fruit Combo
blocks.script: The Globe and Mail reports this week that public menopause care in Canada is scarce, and private care is filling the gap at real cost. In June, the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada warned that a two-tiered health system is emerging in which women are forced to pay for basic health care that should be free. Initial assessments at private and virtual menopause clinics can run $100 to $400. The economic backdrop is substantial: Deloitte Canada's analysis shows menopause costs employers $237 million annually in lost productivity, and costs women $3.3 billion in lost income. For a wealth practice, this is a client conversation about benefits design and women's health coverage, not just a personal health issue.

blocks.title: Jets Stun Canadiens, Raiders Snap Skid
blocks.script: The Winnipeg Jets pulled off one of their best wins of the season last night. Down four to nothing against the Canadiens, they fought all the way back and won in overtime, snapping a nine game losing streak. The Globe and Mail reports the Jets were less than three minutes from a tenth straight defeat before the rally started. That's the kind of result that can turn a season around, and it's worth watching if it sparks a longer run. On the Raiders, Las Vegas ended its own four game skid on Sunday, beating the Jets 38-33 at MetLife Stadium. Kirk Cousins threw three touchdowns and ran for another, and Dylan Laube returned a kickoff 95 yards for a score, the Raiders' first return touchdown since 2011. Las Vegas sits at 4-4 and travels to face the 6-1 49ers this weekend. Elsewhere in the NHL, Lightning star Nikita Kucherov confirmed he requested a trade out of Tampa Bay after 14 years, citing poor communication from management, a stunning move for a reigning Hart Trophy winner. The Devils beat the Oilers in Connor Hellebuyck's first home start with New Jersey, Jack Hughes scoring twice.

Company & Economy Analysis, Statement forensics, lesson 6: Capital expenditure: maintenance versus growth and how to estimate the split.

Here's the number everyone quotes and almost nobody interrogates: capital expenditure, capex, as a line on the cash flow statement. Analysts love to say "capex is forty million, revenue is four hundred million, that's ten percent, fine." But that single figure hides two completely different animals. Maintenance capex keeps the lights on: replacing a worn-out truck, patching a roof, re-lining a furnace. Growth capex buys a second plant. One protects the business you already have. The other is a bet on a bigger one. Lump them together and you can't tell if a company is stagnant and just patching holes, or investing to expand, or worse, starving its own equipment to flatter free cash flow.

There's no line item that splits this for you, so you estimate. The standard method: maintenance capex is roughly equal to depreciation and amortization, adjusted for inflation in asset replacement costs. Take a real one. Union Pacific, fiscal year 2023: depreciation and amortization on the income statement was about 2.3 billion dollars. Total capex that year was roughly 3.6 billion. So maintenance capex, using depreciation as your proxy, is about 2.3 billion, and growth capex is the remaining 1.3 billion, roughly thirty six percent of total spend going toward expansion rather than upkeep. In Thomson ONE, pull depreciation from the income statement tab and total capex from the cash flow statement, both sit right next to each other once you build the comparison.

The mistake people make is assuming depreciation always equals maintenance capex exactly. It doesn't. Depreciation is a historical cost accounting figure, it doesn't account for inflation in replacement equipment prices. For asset-heavy, older-fleet businesses, real maintenance capex often runs higher than depreciation suggests. Treat the depreciation proxy as a floor, not a precise answer.

What this split reveals: capital discipline and the real growth story, separate from management's narrative. What it cannot reveal: whether that growth capex will earn an adequate return. For that you need the next layer, which is what debt financed it and under what terms.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 27: Probate in Manitoba: current fees and what bypasses it.

Manitoba is one of the cheaper provinces for probate, and that surprises most clients who've heard horror stories from Ontario or British Columbia. As of 2026, Manitoba charges a probate fee, technically called a court fee for a grant of probate, of 70 cents per thousand dollars of estate value up to 10 thousand dollars, and then 7 dollars per thousand dollars above that. There's no fee at all on the first 10 thousand. So on an estate worth 800 thousand dollars, you're paying roughly 70 cents times 10, which is 7 dollars, plus 7 dollars per thousand on the remaining 790 thousand, which is 5,530 dollars. Total: about 5,537 dollars. Compare that to Ontario, where the same estate pays over 12,000 dollars in estate administration tax. Manitoba is genuinely low cost by Canadian standards, which changes the conversation with clients who assume probate planning is urgent regardless of province.

Here's what actually bypasses probate, because the fee isn't the only reason to care. Assets with a named beneficiary skip probate entirely: registered accounts like RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs, and life insurance proceeds, as long as a person, not the estate, is named beneficiary. Jointly held property with right of survivorship, common between spouses, passes outside the estate too. So does anything held in a properly funded trust. What stays inside the estate, and therefore inside probate's fee calculation, is anything without a beneficiary designation or joint owner: non-registered investment accounts, real estate held solely, personal property, a private corporation's shares if not otherwise structured.

The one mistake I see constantly: people assume probate fees are the main cost of dying without planning, so they obsess over avoiding a 5,000 dollar fee while ignoring the capital gains tax that triggers on death, which on an incorporated business owner's shares or a cottage property can be tens of thousands of dollars. Probate planning and tax planning are different problems. Don't let one distract from the other.

Communication, lesson 27: Reading the room: nonverbal signals that say the meeting is going wrong.

In 1970, psychologist Albert Mehrabian published research that gets misquoted constantly. People say "ninety three percent of communication is nonverbal." That is not what he found. His study was narrow: it was about feelings and attitudes, specifically when someone's words contradict their tone. In that specific case, tone and body carried more weight than the words. It was never a universal law. But the narrower claim still matters for you, because in a client meeting, the contradiction between words and body is exactly your warning signal.

Here is the pattern to watch. Three cues cluster together when a meeting is going wrong: torso turning toward the door or away from you, a drop in verbal backchannel ("mm-hmm," "right," "okay") for more than fifteen seconds, and a change in blink rate, usually faster, which research by Joe Tecce at Boston College linked to stress and cognitive load during the 1996 presidential debates. Any one of these alone means little. People shift in chairs because chairs are uncomfortable. But when you get two or three stacking inside sixty seconds, that is the room going wrong.

The one mistake: treating silence as agreement. A client who stops asking questions is not necessarily satisfied. On a board call, if a member goes quiet and stops nodding but keeps eye contact, that is often confusion they are too polite to admit, not consent.

Here is the worked moment. You are forty minutes into a pitch. At minute twelve you asked "does this make sense so far" and got three head nods and a verbal "yep." At minute thirty five you ask again and get silence, a slight lean back, and one glance at a phone on the table. That is not boredom, per communications researcher Nick Morgan's work on audience disengagement. That is a cue to stop presenting and ask a direct question.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pull one company's depreciation and total capex from Thomson ONE for the last two fiscal years, calculate the implied growth capex percentage, and note whether it's rising or falling year over year.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull one client's most recent estate summary and calculate their actual Manitoba probate fee by hand using the 70 cents and 7 dollars per thousand brackets, then note which of their assets would bypass probate entirely.

Communication: In your next client or board call, track one listener for silence longer than fifteen seconds combined with torso turning away. When you spot both together, pause and ask an open question within ten seconds.

blocks.title: TFSAs Drain, OAS Shrinks, CIRO Tightens Rules
blocks.script:
Two retirement income stories landed today that belong in your next client meeting. The C.D. Howe Institute finds Old Age Security now covers a shrinking share of what retirees actually need, part of a broader erosion in how much benefits and workplace pensions replace of career earnings. Pair that with new data the Globe and Mail reports today showing Canadians are draining their TFSAs faster, with young and old both tapping accounts, young people for family costs, older clients for retirement income gaps. If you have clients treating the TFSA as an emergency fund rather than a growth vehicle, this is your opening to talk about contribution room they're giving up permanently.

On the regulatory side, CIRO posted three new unpaid fines today. Josephine Sudario in Ontario owes 615,000 dollars from a May decision. Debojyoti Majumder owes 75,000 dollars from July. Christina Cole in British Columbia owes just over 59,000 dollars, also from July. Worth checking if any of these names cross your referral network.

Separately, CIRO released draft guidance telling dealers to stop overreaching with non-disclosure agreements in client settlements. The guidance says confidentiality clauses can't block clients from talking to regulators, and settlements need plain language clients actually understand. If your firm uses NDAs in complaint resolution, expect compliance to revisit templates.

On the budget front, Thursday's federal budget already confirmed small-business tax measures are coming. The piece incorporated business owners should watch is the Productivity Mega Deduction, 36 billion dollars over five years letting companies immediately write off more capital investment. That matters for physicians and other incorporated professionals weighing equipment or practice purchases before year end.

And on rates, last week's Bank of Canada hike to 2.5 percent means variable mortgage clients need a payment review now, not in January.

blocks.title: Sewage Spill, Severance Payouts, and a Mine Fire
blocks.script:
Start with the Red River. The City of Winnipeg says nearly 10 million litres of raw sewage spilled into the river early Monday morning. Two automated bypass gates at the North End sewage treatment plant opened unexpectedly at about 1:10 a.m., allowing untreated wastewater to spill into the river, with the city estimating 9.8 megalitres of sewage spilled. That's smaller than the 230 million litre Fort Garry Bridge spill from last year, but it's another infrastructure embarrassment right as a new council takes its seats, and if you sit on an environmental or infrastructure committee, expect this to come up.

Speaking of the new council, nine new faces get sworn in today, and that turnover comes with a price tag. CBC reports a record number of departing Winnipeg councillors, nine of them, are eligible for a combined total of about 525 thousand dollars in severance after last week's civic election. That's taxpayer money going out the door as the city grapples with its own infrastructure and budget pressures, a point worth raising if you're advising anyone on municipal bonds or city finances.

Up north, a fire broke out underground at the T3 mine in Thompson Thursday. The mine's owner, Exiro Metals, confirmed there was a fire involving a piece of equipment, and as a precaution, employees underground followed established safety procedures and went to designated safety locations while the mine rescue team extinguished the fire. No injuries, operations resumed after the area was confirmed safe. Worth flagging for anyone with exposure to northern Manitoba mining names.
